interactions.summary: Jiang checks that the class sees cheating as the breaking of a real bond rather than a private lapse, and keeps pushing the trust logic of the example.
A student frames covenant as a bond whose violation carries a death-price logic, and Jiang sharpens the point by saying the central wound is the collapse of trust into suspicion.
A student proposes that divine judgment differs from human romance because God can see whether repentance is genuine in a way a boyfriend or girlfriend cannot.

claims.claim: Jiang treats cheating as the breaking of an actual bond created by vow, not merely as a sexual act that happened to occur.
A student defines covenant as a bond whose breach carries sacrificial or death-price consequences, invoking biblical imagery to explain why the violation is so serious.
Jiang argues that the deepest damage in an affair is not sex itself but the shift from a relationship of trust to one structured by suspicion.
A student proposes that God is a better judge of repentance than a romantic partner because God can see the whole self and know whether change is real.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang snaps the whole adultery discussion into focus by relocating the offense from sex to trust.
signature_moments.source_phrase: The sex is not the issue. The affair is not the issue. The trust is the issue.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's cleanest compression of why vow-breaking matters: the visible act matters because it mutates the underlying relation.

signature_moments.moment: The student contrasts human uncertainty with divine omniscience: lovers can be persuaded or unconvinced, but God can see whether inner change is real.
signature_moments.source_phrase: your boyfriend or girlfriend cannot read your mind
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It offers the class its first concrete account of why God might redeem where human relationships stay trapped in suspicion.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The relational tie created by vow; cheating matters because it breaks this bond rather than merely violating a rule.
A vow-bound relationship understood in biblical terms as carrying grave consequence if broken.
The real substance of the relationship for Jiang here; betrayal converts it into suspicion.

chronology_notes.note: The discussion advances from covenant and public vow toward the more precise claim that betrayal destroys trust, while also opening the contrast between human suspicion and divine insight.
